title: Hierarchical models and shrinkage
objectives: Pool many strategies’ hit rates with a hierarchical model and see the shrinkage.

screens.title: Twelve hit rates
screens.prose: Twelve strategies have win rates from 0.40 to 0.70, on 20 to 400 trades each. Rank them by eye. Then raise $\kappa$: each rate is pulled towards 0.5417 as if it had $\kappa$ extra trades at that rate.

derive.caption: $\kappa$ = {{round(kap, 1)}}: the 20-trade strategy keeps weight {{fixed(20/(20 + kap), 3)}} on its own record

screens.question: At $\kappa = 0$ the top strategy is the 50-trade one at 0.70. Set $\kappa = 43$. Which is top now?

options.why: Its 50 trades carry about half the weight at $\kappa = 43$, so it falls to 0.627.
With 20 trades it keeps weight 0.32 and drops to 0.560.

feedback.correct: The 300-trade strategy, whose 0.687 barely moves, now leads.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\kappa = 43$ and look at the top two points.

byKey.same: You kept the raw ranking. The 50-trade record shrinks much more than the 300-trade one.

explain.text: At $\kappa = 43$ the 50-trade rate falls from 0.70 to 0.627. The 300-trade one only falls from 0.687 to 0.668.

screens.title: A model for all twelve
screens.prose: A **hierarchical model** says each hit rate is drawn from a population: $p_j \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ and $k_j \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_j, p_j)$. Fitting $a$ and $b$ to all twelve gives $\hat a = 23.31$ and $\hat b = 19.72$, so $\hat\kappa = 43.02$. Strategy $j$ keeps weight $n_j/(n_j + \hat\kappa)$ on its own record.

state.caption: Raw rates (orange) and shrunk rates (black) at $\hat\kappa = 43.02$

screens.question: What weight does the 20-trade strategy keep on its own record?

feedback.correct: 0.317: two thirds of its estimate comes from the population.

byKey.prior: That is the weight on the population mean.
byKey.a: You used $\hat a = 23.31$ alone. The prior's strength is $\hat a + \hat b$.

screens.title: Empirical Bayes
screens.prose: Integrating out each $p_j$ makes $k_j$ beta-binomial. Maximising that likelihood over $a$ and $b$ is **empirical Bayes**. A `betaln` likelihood with Nelder-Mead and `betabinom.logpmf` with L-BFGS-B agree within 0.02. The population mean is $23.31/43.02 = 0.5417$; the pooled rate is 0.5501.

state.caption: Raw rates (orange) and shrunk rates (black) at $\hat\kappa = 43.02$

screens.question: What is the shrunk hit rate of the strategy with 35 wins in 50 trades?

hints.text: Add $\hat a$ to the wins and $\hat\kappa$ to the trades.

byKey.pool: You shrank towards the pooled 0.5501. The model shrinks towards 0.5417.

screens.title: Closer to the truth
screens.prose: The data were simulated, so the true rates are known. The mean squared error against them is 0.00558 for the raw rates and 0.00272 for the shrunk ones.

state.caption: Raw rates (orange) and shrunk rates (black) at $\hat\kappa = 43.02$

screens.question: By what factor does shrinkage cut the mean squared error?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the raw error by the shrunk one.

explain.text: $0.0055811/0.0027197 = 2.05$. The noisy small samples gain most.

screens.title: Ten fund alphas
screens.prose: Ten funds report alphas $\hat\alpha_j$ with standard errors $s_j$ from 1.5% to 5%. Take $\hat\alpha_j \sim N(\alpha_j, s_j^2)$ and $\alpha_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)$. The marginal likelihood gives $\hat\mu = 2.2478$ and $\hat\tau = 1.6943$. Each estimate moves towards $\hat\mu$ by $B_j = s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \hat\tau^2)$.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: Fund 10 reports 12.26% with standard error 5%. What is its shrunk alpha, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shrink the gap to $\hat\mu$ by $B_{10} = 0.897$.

byKey.b: You kept $B$ of the gap, not $1 - B$.

screens.title: Allocate to the top fund
screens.prose: A platform ranks the ten funds by reported alpha. The top one, fund 10 at 12.26%, gets the most capital. Its standard error is 5%, the largest in the table.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: What is wrong with the ranking?

options.text: The noisiest fund tops it: extremes are mostly noise, and after shrinkage fund 1 leads
Nothing: 12.26% is the best estimate of fund 10's alpha
options.why: Alone it is unbiased, but chosen as the top of ten it is biased upwards. Its shrunk alpha is 3.28%.
That ranks by evidence against zero, not by size of alpha. Shrinkage gives the expected alpha.

hints.text: Which funds can post extreme numbers by luck?
Those with the largest standard errors.

feedback.correct: The best of many noisy tries is mostly luck, as in `limits-thm` lesson 17.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which fund's figure is most noise?

byKey.fine: You trusted the raw top. Selected as the maximum, it overstates the fund's alpha.

explain.text: Fund 10's 12.26% shrinks to 3.28% and fund 1's 5.08% to 3.84%, so the order flips. Against the true alphas the error falls from 10.58 to 4.88.

screens.title: One factor for all
screens.prose: A colleague shrinks every fund halfway to $\hat\mu$, whatever its standard error. Drag $\tau$ and watch the arrows: the hierarchical model shrinks each fund by its own $B_j$.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: Why is one common factor wrong?

options.text: A fund measured precisely deserves less shrinkage than a noisy one: $B_j$ rises with $s_j$
It is fine if the factor is chosen well
options.why: No single factor fits both fund 1 ($B = 0.44$) and fund 10 ($B = 0.90$).

options.text: Precise funds should shrink more, as they are closer to $\mu$
options.why: Precision means the estimate is closer to its own true alpha, not to $\mu$.

hints.text: Shrinkage must follow each fund's noise.

feedback.correct: Shrink each estimate by its own noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does $B_j$ depend on?

byKey.ok: You thought one factor could fit. The factors run from 0.44 to 0.90.

explain.text: $B_j = s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \hat\tau^2)$ runs from 0.4394 for fund 1 to 0.8970 for fund 10.

screens.title: Where the shrinkage factor comes from
screens.prose: Combine one fund's estimate with the population prior, as in lesson 14. Leave out the slip.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Prior $\alpha_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)$ and estimate $\hat\alpha_j \mid \alpha_j \sim N(\alpha_j, s_j^2)$, the two levels of the model
Multiply top and bottom by $s_j^2\tau^2$: $\frac{s_j^2\mu + \tau^2\hat\alpha_j}{s_j^2 + \tau^2} = \mu + (1 - B_j)(\hat\alpha_j - \mu)$ with $B_j = \frac{s_j^2}{s_j^2 + \tau^2}$
Posterior mean $\frac{\mu\tau^2 + \hat\alpha_j s_j^2}{\tau^2 + s_j^2}$, weighting each by its variance
lines.why: That weights by variance, so the noisier piece would count more. Weights are precisions.

hints.text: Precisions add and weight the means.

feedback.correct: $B_j$ is the share of the total variance that is noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight by precision, then simplify.

byKey.x: You weighted by variances. The noisier estimate would then count more.

explain.text: With $s_{10} = 5$ and $\tau = 1.6943$, $B_{10} = 25/27.87 = 0.897$, so fund 10 keeps about a tenth of its gap from $\hat\mu$.

screens.title: When $\tau$ hits zero
screens.prose: Rerun the fund model on a second planted table (seed 101). The marginal likelihood is highest at $\hat\tau = 0$, so every fund shrinks to $\hat\mu = -0.80$. A full Bayesian fit puts a prior on $\mu$ and $\tau$ and samples them with lesson 16's sampler. Lesson 17's checks then apply.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: What does $\hat\tau = 0$ tell us?

options.text: The data cannot tell the funds apart; it does not prove their alphas are equal
All ten funds have exactly the same alpha
options.why: An estimate of 0 says the spread is too small to detect here. It does not say the spread is zero.
A maximum at the boundary is a valid answer. A full Bayesian fit would give $\tau$ a posterior instead.

hints.text: How big are the standard errors next to any plausible $\tau$?
Small true differences are invisible at that noise.

feedback.correct: Complete pooling is a statement about the evidence, not about the funds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would a small true spread look like at these errors?

byKey.equal: You read $\hat\tau = 0$ as proof. It only says the spread is not detectable.

explain.text: With errors of 1.5% to 5%, a true spread of 1% barely changes the likelihood. A posterior for $\tau$ would keep mass above 0, so the funds stay apart a little.

screens.prose: Fit both models by maximising the marginal likelihood with `scipy.optimize.minimize` on the log scale, so the parameters stay positive. For the alphas, optimise $(\mu, \ln\tau)$ and return the posterior means.

screens.title: A multi-manager platform
screens.prose: A multi-manager platform allocates capital to 40 portfolio managers by measured alpha. Track records run from six months to eight years. Ridge regression in `stat-learning` lesson 7 shrank every coefficient towards 0 with one penalty.

derive.caption: $\tau$ = {{fixed(tau, 2)}}: arrows run from reported (orange) to shrunk (black)

screens.question: What should the platform allocate on?

options.text: Each manager's alpha shrunk by its own noise towards the platform's mean, as in the fund model
The measured alphas, since they are unbiased
options.why: The top of 40 noisy records is biased upwards; short records dominate the extremes.

options.text: Ridge with one common penalty for every manager
options.why: Ridge is the same shrinkage with one $\tau$ and equal noise. Records of different lengths need their own $B_j$.

feedback.correct: Shrink each record by its noise, then allocate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a six-month record's alpha mostly contain?

byKey.ridge: You chose one common penalty. That fits equal noise; these records differ in length.

explain.text: Ridge is a normal prior with one $\tau$ on equally noisy coefficients. The hierarchical model lets the data choose $\tau$ and gives each manager its own $B_j$.

ideas: A hierarchical model draws each strategy's rate from a population whose parameters all strategies estimate together.
Each estimate moves towards the population mean by its own noise: weight $n_j/(n_j + \hat\kappa)$, or $1 - B_j$ for alphas.
When the units share one population, shrunk estimates beat raw ones on average: fund 10's 12.26% becomes 3.28%.

formula.name: Normal shrinkage
formula.note: Fitted by the marginal likelihood $\hat\alpha_j \sim N(\mu, s_j^2 + \tau^2)$.

summary.trap: Ranking by raw estimates: the noisiest fund tops the table because noise makes the extremes.

quiz.prose: A fund's alpha has standard error 3%. The population of alphas has $\hat\tau = 2\%$.
quiz.question: What is its shrinkage factor $B$?

byKey.inv: That is $\tau^2/(s^2 + \tau^2)$, the weight on the fund's own estimate.
byKey.sd: You used standard deviations, $3/5$. Use variances.

explain.text: $B = 9/(9 + 4) = 0.6923$: the estimate keeps 31% of its gap from $\hat\mu$.

quiz.question: What is its shrunk hit rate?

byKey.20: You expected the small sample to stay high. It shrinks most.
